name: Pre-Christian Kongo religion (Nzambi/bisimbi/minkisi)

dating.dating_summary: Nearly everything popularly stated about "precolonial Kongo religion" is actually late-19th/early-20th-century ethnography (the Laman manuscript collection, c. 1915, written by Protestant converts) or the missionary-syncretic vocabulary retrojected backward; treat pre-1483 Kongo religious content as substantially reconstructed, not directly documented.

earliest_archaeological_evidence.note: The Kongo Kingdom's traditional founding (Lukeni lua Nimi, c. 1390) rests on genealogical/oral reconstruction, not archaeology; no specific dated excavated site for pre-contact religious material culture was verified in this research pass.

earliest_written_attestation.note: Portuguese contact from 1483 (Diogo Cão); these are external/colonial observer accounts, not Kongo-authored texts, and post-date any actual founding of the religious system by an unknown span.

surviving_manuscript_date.note: Karl Laman's ~10,000-page manuscript collection from Protestant converts, c. 1915 — over 400 years after first European contact, and already shaped by the missionary encounter.

tradition_internal_claim.note: No single canonical origin narrative recoverable; oral traditions on kingdom founding vary by clan/dynastic line (Kimpanzu/Kinlaza/Kwilu).

estimated_oral_origin.method: Jan Vansina's comparative-historical-linguistics/Bantu-expansion dating places the general ancestor-veneration/nkisi-type cultural substrate as considerably older than the Kongo kingdom itself, plausibly first-millennium-CE Bantu-speaking Central Africa — a linguistic-reconstruction inference, not a hard date.

notes: DISPUTED: whether Nzambi a Mpungu was originally a benevolent creator/sky-father (older ethnographic synthesis, e.g. Fu-Kiau) or originally a personification of death, with the life/creation valence instead carried by bisimbi (chthonic land/water spirit forces) — per Wyatt MacGaffey, "Precolonial Beliefs in God, Nzambi, and Chthonic Beings: Evidence from Kongo Texts," Journal of Religion in Africa 52(1-2), 2022, using the Laman manuscripts. See claim_nzambi_meaning_disputed. "Fetish" (from Portuguese feitiço) is a documented colonial mistranslation of nkisi/minkisi — MacGaffey, "Fetishism Revisited: Kongo Nkisi in Sociological Perspective," Africa journal.
